tier_reason: README Performance section gives the second-order table (HyperJet static 15/101/921/12,214 ns vs Eigen AutoDiffScalar nested 18/328/2,888/22,105 and autodiff dual2nd 127/375/2,425/17,679) and the first-order table, measured on an Apple M1 Pro with Apple clang 21.0.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG; the benchmark code is public at benchmark/compare/compare.cpp (Compare target in benchmark/CMakeLists.txt, Google Benchmark 1.9.1, Eigen 3.4.0, autodiff v1.1.2, Ceres 2.2.0) and checks all contenders agree before timing.

corrections.caveats: Author-run benchmark on a single Apple Silicon machine, but the benchmark code (benchmark/compare/compare.cpp) is in the repository, pins dependency versions, and verifies that every contender produces the same value, gradient and Hessian before timing. The README is candid that there is no gain for gradient-only work (HyperJet 244 vs AutoDiffScalar 245 vs ceres::Jet 304 ns at n=24) and that the dynamic-size HyperJet variant is far slower (644 ns at n=3, 22,777 ns at n=24). The Eigen baseline is AutoDiffScalar from Eigen's unsupported module, not Eigen Tensor. compare.cpp forces always_inline uniformly for all contenders because inlining decisions change absolute times by about 1.6x. Small project (17 stars); library requires C++23.

notes: All claimed numbers match the README tables exactly; ratios 3.3x (n=6), 2.6x (n=12), 1.5x (n=24), 1.2x (n=3) are the README's own. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 17 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-28 (benchmark added that day in PR #90).

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed comparison (ADBench paper; the source says shorter versions appeared at AD2016 and in Optimization Methods and Software, Feb 2018) with absolute-runtime tables for BA and GMM where Adept beats ADOL-C and Ceres; benchmark code is public in microsoft/ADBench and the CPU (Xeon E5-1620 @ 3.60GHz, Windows 10) is stated, but no compiler or flags, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Bundle adjustment Jacobian, smallest instance (3.18e+04 measurements): Adept 6.79e-02 vs ADOL-C 8.50e-01 vs Ceres 2.26e-01 (about 12.5x and 3.3x faster, derived from page data); largest instance (2.90e+07): Adept 6.63e+01 vs ADOL-C 7.09e+02 (about 10.7x, derived from page data); Ceres crashed on that instance (bullet in the table). GMM 10k points, 30 parameters: Adept (split) 2.86e-02 vs ADOL-C (split) 4.71e-01 (about 16x, derived from page data), but unsplit Adept 1.70e-02 vs unsplit ADOL-C 3.08e-02 is only about 1.8x (derived from page data). Hand-written C++ derivative was still about 3.5x faster than Adept on BA (1.96e-02 vs 6.79e-02).
corrections.caveats: The ADBench paper used the newest tool versions available in July-August 2015, i.e. Adept 1.1 (June 2015 per the Adept-2 ChangeLog), not Adept 2.x (2.0 released September 2017); the Adept-2 README claims it is as fast as Adept 1.1 but that is first-party. Compiler and flags are not stated. On GMM without manual splitting ADOL-C was faster than Adept at some sizes (330 parameters: 8.79e-02 vs 9.61e-02; 3,300: 8.49e-01 vs 9.76e-01; 10,700: 1.90 vs 3.11), unsplit Adept crashed at 429k parameters and unsplit ADOL-C crashed from 21.5k parameters up. Ceres is forward-mode only in this test, which disadvantages it. Tapenade (C source transformation) was faster than Adept on both GMM and BA. The table captions do not restate the time unit. Adept is not the incumbent in this category's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor). ADBench repository is archived (July 2024).

notes: Every cited number is in the ms.tex tables (tab:ba-abs, tab:gmm-10k-abs); fixed 'Ceres did not finish' to 'crashed' (bullet = crash per caption) and added the much smaller unsplit GMM ratio. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0 core (test/ and benchmark/ under GNU all-permissive), 189 stars, not archived, last commit 2025-10-05.

tier_reason: Well-known independent shootout (soumith/convnet-benchmarks) lists Nervana-neon fp16/fp32 rows beside CuDNN[R4] fp16/fp32 on an i7-5930K + Titan X; the benchmark script (nervana/convnet-benchmarks.py) and logs are public but no compiler, flags or library versions are stated, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Numbers compare against cuDNN R4 only; later cuDNN releases added Winograd and other algorithms, so today's gap is likely smaller or reversed (not measured here). The suite states CPU and GPU but no compiler, flags or driver versions. The suite's nervana/README.md says Nervana provided limited-release beta kernels, and its nervana/convnet-benchmarks.py imports the standalone nervanagpu package (convnew branch, kernels assembled with maxas) rather than neon itself; neon later carries a NervanaGPU backend (neon/backends/nervanagpu.py, layer_gpu.py 'mainly used for old benchmarking code'), so the lineage is the same but identical kernels are not confirmed. The fast kernels are hand-written GPU assembly (SASS) driven from Python, not C++. neon's README claims '2x speed of cuDNNv4'; the page shows 1.0-2.0x depending on model and cuDNN wins AlexNet. Repository archived 2023-01-03 with an Intel discontinuation notice.

notes: All neon and cuDNN R4 numbers match the convnet-benchmarks README rows (fp16 figures also match nervana/output_fp16.log). Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0, 3.9k stars, archived 2023-01-03, last commit 2019-05-22. Key shortcoming: benchmarked code is the nervanagpu beta-kernel package, not the neon repository as such.
